Omega
oh-MAY-guh
n.
From Greek omega (ω, Ω), the last and largest of the Greek vowels; its name means “big O” (o mega) to distinguish it from omicron (“little o”). As the final letter of the Greek alphabet, omega became a natural symbol for ending, completion, and ultimate reality across Hellenistic literature and into Christian theology.

Biblical Definition

Omega receives its supreme theological weight when the risen and glorified Christ claims it as the other bookend of His eternal identity: “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, “who is, and who was, and who is to come — the Almighty” (Rev 1:8). If alpha declares Christ's absolute primacy as the uncaused Beginning, omega declares His absolute finality as the uncircumventable End. History does not fade into an open horizon; it arrives at a Person. Every process, every age, every judgment, every glory terminates in the One who says “I am the Omega.” At Revelation 22:13 the title is compounded into a triad: “I am the Alpha and the Omega — the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End” — the same divine sovereignty declared three different ways to establish it beyond all question. The apocalyptic context is deliberate: the last letter of the alphabet is spoken by the One who presides over the last things. Every eschatological hope — the resurrection, the new creation, the marriage supper of the Lamb, the tree of life, the river of life — flows from the One who is the Omega: “It is done. I am the Alpha and the Omega — the Beginning and the End” (Rev 21:6). When the last seal is opened, the last trumpet sounds, and the last judgment is pronounced, the voice that speaks is the voice of the Omega — not an impersonal process but the Son of God who holds the last word over every life, every nation, and every age. The Omega is not merely the endpoint but the telos: the purposeful End toward which all of redemptive history has been moving.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) records omega as the last letter of the Greek alphabet, the natural symbol of finality and completion; in Christian theology it names the risen Christ as the absolute End and purposeful Telos of all created history.

expand to see more

OMEGA, n. [Gr. ω, or Ω; “great O.”] The last letter of the Greek alphabet, corresponding to the long O in English. As the final letter, omega became in classical and Hellenistic usage a symbol for “the last,” “the end,” or “the ultimate.” Webster notes its derivation distinguishing it from omicron, the short form.

In Scripture, omega functions as one half of Christ's self-designation as the complete span of all reality: from the Alpha (beginning) to the Omega (end) there is nothing outside His sovereign knowledge and governance. The title belongs to God alone in Isa 44:6 and its New Testament appropriation by Christ is a claim to divinity that Revelation's first readers would have recognized immediately.

Key Scripture

Revelation 22:13 — "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last."

Revelation 1:8 — "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord, which is, and which was, and which is to come, the Almighty."

Revelation 21:6 — "And he said unto me, It is done. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end. I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely."

Hebrews 12:2 — "Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God."

Modern Corruption

Existentialist and postmodern thought resists the Omega by insisting that history has no telos, no purposeful end, no divine tribunal; therapeutic culture replaces the Omega-judgment with self-actualization as the only “end” that matters; New Age cosmology reinterprets omega as a cyclical return rather than a definitive conclusion.

expand to see more

Pierre Teilhard de Chardin's “Omega Point” reinterprets the biblical title as an evolutionary telos — an impersonal convergence of cosmic consciousness toward which all matter is rising. This is a sophisticated corruption: it borrows the apostolic symbol while replacing the personal, judging God of Revelation with a pantheistic attractor. The Omega of Revelation does not evolve toward us; He descends to judge. He does not emerge from the process; He terminates it by His sovereign word.

Postmodern philosophy explicitly rejects teleology — the idea that history has a purposeful end. On this account there is no Omega, only an endless deferral of meaning. The biblical answer is not a philosophical counter-argument but a Person: the One who says “It is done” (Rev 21:6) and then names Himself the Omega. History ends not when it runs out of steam but when the One who holds its final syllable speaks it. The church lives between the Alpha and the Omega — not in metaphysical anxiety about whether there is an end, but in confident hope that the End has a name, a face, and a throne.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Omega, the last and largest Greek vowel, inherited the natural symbolism of finality from its position in the alphabet; Scripture elevated this mundane grammatical fact into a cosmic declaration of Christ's sovereignty over all created endings.

expand to see more

Greek omega (ω/Ω) — from o mega, “big O,” the 24th and last letter of the Greek alphabet.

Greek omicron (ο) — contrasted with omega; the “small o” that forced the distinction and gave omega its name.

Septuagint and New Testament Greek — in which Christ's self-declarations in Revelation are written, making the last letter of the Greek alphabet serve as His cosmic title.

Patristic exegesis — the Fathers read Alpha-Omega as confirming Christ's consubstantial divinity with the Father who declares Himself “the first and the last” in Isaiah (Isa 44:6; 48:12).

English omega — used to designate the ultimate, the final, or the extreme expression of anything; its biblical origin is often forgotten but the semantic weight of “finality” survives.

Usage

"The Omega title is eschatological at its core: it belongs to the One before whom every created thing will give account, and whose word closes every age — not as an abstract principle of ending but as the living Judge who speaks “It is done” at the consummation."

"Hebrews 12:2 describes Christ as “the author and perfecter of faith” — the One who initiates saving faith in the elect and brings it to its final completion: an explication of Omega-lordship applied to the individual believer's spiritual journey from regeneration to glorification."

"The threefold title “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last.” (Rev 22:13) leaves no interval of existence, no epoch of history, no creature's life outside the sovereignty of Christ: He owns every syllable from first to last."
